cases.title: Apia Park stadium rehabilitation: a worker killed and two hurt moving beams
cases.place: Apia Park sports complex, Apia, Samoa
cases.point: Apia Park sports complex (OpenStreetMap way 666117780), the coordinate AidData's own location narrative gives for the project. The accident happened on the stadium works at that site.

lenders.name: China Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM)
lenders.role: AidData record 64861. This was a grant, not a loan: RMB 43,000,000 ($6,900,000) provided to the Government of Samoa on 28 March 2005 for the Apia Park Stadium Rehabilitation Project, which AidData values at $11,389,289 in constant 2021 dollars. MOFCOM was the project sponsor, carried out the final project inspection on 12 March 2007, and the works were handed over to the Samoan authorities on 3 April 2007. The same record notes that the interest-free Chinese loan which had financed the original stadium, built between 1981 and 1983 for the 1983 South Pacific Games, was forgiven in 2006. No World Bank P-number exists for this financing.

cases.conditions: The grant was spent through a Chinese contractor rather than paid to Samoa to procure with: a project design contract was signed in early 2005 at a ceremony attended by Prime Minister Tuilaepa, Samoa's Minister of Engineering, the Chinese ambassador Liu Guanren and the head of the Economic and Commercial Office, Zhou Geping, and on 13 December 2005 a project implementation contract was signed with Qingjian Group, which AidData says was then called Qingdao Construction Group Corporation. Groundbreaking was on 17 February 2006 and the Chinese ministry that provided the money also signed off the finished works. AidData's own record names the contractor two ways: its description names Qingjian Group (then Qingdao Construction Group Corporation), while its implementing-agency field reads "Chongqing Construction Engineering Group|Government of Samoa". RNZ Pacific spells the contractor Qindao Construction Group Ltd (AidData record 64861; RNZ Pacific).

companies.name: Qingjian Group (formerly Qingdao Construction Group Corporation)
companies.role: Held the project implementation contract signed on 13 December 2005 and was carrying out the stadium works when the fatal accident happened. RNZ Pacific spells the name Qindao Construction Group Ltd and gives its general manager as Hai Wang

cases.community: Samoa asked China to repair and expand the stadium so that it could host the opening and closing ceremonies of the 2007 South Pacific Games. The works reinforced the stands, renovated a runway, added stands, VIP boxes and tennis courts (AidData record 64861). In February 2007, during those works, a worker was killed and two others were hurt. AidData's record says a Chinese engineer was killed when he fell from a machine being used to install beams for the stadium, that a second Chinese engineer was hospitalised after being severely injured in the same incident, and that a Samoan worker was also injured. RNZ Pacific, reporting on a claim that the deaths were being covered up, says a Chinese man was killed and two other workers injured in an incident "in February" during construction of the stadium, and that the Games organisers' account of the accident has a beam being moved during the works when it happened. Leulua'ialii Olinda Woodroffe, a New Zealand-based Samoan lawyer, said someone was trying to cover the incident up, and that Qindao Construction Group Ltd had hired her to investigate the death and the injuries. The chief executive of the South Pacific Games, Fonoti Manogiamanu Etuale, said police had thoroughly investigated the incident and denied that there had been any cover-up of the Chinese worker’s death; he said the construction company's general manager, Hai Wang, had told him the lawyer was hired to help recover an insurance claim on a damaged beam that was being moved when the fatal accident happened (RNZ Pacific). Neither source names the dead man, and neither gives a day in February.
cases.killed_note: One worker killed on the stadium works. AidData has a Chinese engineer killed by a fall from a machine installing beams, with a second Chinese engineer hospitalised with severe injuries and a Samoan worker also injured; RNZ Pacific has one Chinese man killed and two other workers injured. The dead man is not named in either source, and the two injuries are counted nowhere as a figure of their own.
cases.outcome: The Chinese ministry that funded the works carried out its final inspection on 12 March 2007, five weeks or so after the accident, and the stadium was handed over to the Samoan authorities on 3 April 2007 and used for the Games that year (AidData record 64861). The Games chief executive said police had investigated the death thoroughly; no police, coroner's or labour-inspection finding on it is held here, and whether the dead man's family or the injured men were paid anything is not established, beyond the Games chief executive's account that the lawyer's instructions concerned an insurance claim on the damaged beam (RNZ Pacific). AidData records a later controversy over the complex: citing the Lowy Institute and several media reports, it says Samoa could not meet the recurring cost of maintaining the swimming pool at the Aquatic Centre and asked New Zealand to carry it.

sources.title: RNZ Pacific report on the Apia Park stadium works (the page carries no headline, byline or date): a lawyer alleges a cover-up of a Chinese worker's death and the South Pacific Games chief executive answers that police investigated thoroughly
AidData Global Chinese Development Finance Dataset, record 64861: Chinese Government provides RMB 43 million grant for Apia Park Stadium Rehabilitation Project
Cablegate: Chinese Growing Investments in Samoa (Wellington 000773)

cases.confidence_note: The death is carried outside AidData by one source: an RNZ Pacific report of a lawyer's cover-up claim and the Games chief executive's answer to it, which gives one man killed, two workers injured, the contractor's name and a beam being moved during the works when the fatal accident happened. That page carries no date and says only "in February"; February 2007 is AidData's date, not the report's. AidData's record is the only place here that gives the fall from a beam-installing machine, the second engineer's hospitalisation and the Samoan worker's injury; the 2007 Pacific Islands Report article it cites for them, "1 DEAD, 2 HURT IN APIA GAMES PROJECT ACCIDENT", is not held here. The two sources also spell the contractor differently, and AidData's own implementing-agency field names a different company again, so which firm employed the dead man is not settled. The US embassy cable of 25 October 2007 carries only the Chinese low-interest loans and grants for the main Games venues, and the Samoa Chamber of Commerce president’s statement that the loans for the sports complexes had since been forgiven; it does not name Apia Park and says nothing about the accident. No inquiry finding and no compensation record is held here.
cx: Chinese government grant for the Apia Park stadium rehabilitation
cases.whole: The grant paid for the main venue of the 2007 South Pacific Games: reinforced stands, a renovated runway, extra stands, VIP boxes and tennis courts at a complex China had built in the first place, between 1981 and 1983, with an interest-free loan for the 1983 Games, and had funded a run of maintenance and renovation projects on since. That loan was forgiven in 2006. Samoa then could not meet the running costs of what it had been given: AidData, citing the Lowy Institute and several media reports, says the government could not finance the recurring cost of maintaining the Aquatic Centre swimming pool and asked New Zealand to shoulder it (AidData record 64861).

codesc.name: AVIC International Holding Corporation
codesc.desc: Chinese company whose business, as the UK register of overseas companies states it, is international aviation, trade and logistics, and real estate and hotel management, from an address in Chaoyang District, Beijing; the same register records its former name as China National Aero-Technology Import & Export Corporation, to 25 October 2010. A Hong Kong Stock Exchange circular of 25 October 2019 calls it a limited liability company established in the PRC and the holding company and a controlling shareholder of the Hong Kong-listed AVIC International Holdings Limited.

sources.title: Company Overview for AVIC INTERNATIONAL HOLDING CORPORATION (FC028179)
AVIC International Holdings Limited: circular — very substantial disposal and deemed disposal of interest in Tian Ma
sources.publisher: The Stock Exchange of Hong Kong (HKEXnews)

codesc.note: Checked. Companies House FC028179 re-opened and confirmed field by field: name exactly as the case key has it, 'Incorporated in: CHINA', 'Legal form: Limited', 'Objects of the company: International aviation, trade and logistic, real estate & hotels management', 'Overseas company address: Avic Intl.Plaza/No.18, Beichen East Rd, Chaoyang District, Beijing 100101, China', 'Parent registry: State Administration For Industry And Commerce Of The People'S Republic Of China', previous name China National Aero-Technology Import & Export Corporation 01 Nov 2007 – 25 Oct 2010. CORRECTED: the writer's 'registered in Beijing'. The register gives a national parent registry (SAIC of the PRC) and a Beijing address; it nowhere says the company is registered in Beijing. Rewritten as the address the register gives. ADDED, from a source the writer named only to rule out: the HKEX circular of 25 October 2019 for AVIC International Holdings Limited defines 'AVIC International' as 'a limited liability company established in the PRC, and a controlling Shareholder', and its indebtedness statement names 'AVIC International Holding Corporation (the holding company of the Company)'. That is the company in the key, described as the parent of the Hong Kong-listed entity, so it is not fault 2 — the direction runs the right way. Still deliberately not written, because no page opened says it of the company in the key: state ownership, a parent (Aviation Industry Corporation of China), an incorporation date, a revenue or employee figure, a product range. The circular gives no shareholding percentage, so none is given. Companies House 'First UK establishment opened on 1 November 2007' is a UK establishment date, not an incorporation date, and is not used.

codesc.name: Shanghai Municipal Engineering Design Institute (Group) Co., Ltd
codesc.desc: Chinese design firm in Shanghai. Engineering News-Record's 2017 ranking of Chinese design firms placed it 12th by total design revenue, at $367.13 million; the list does not say which year that revenue covers.
codesc.note: Checked. ENR table re-opened: headings '2017 Rank | 2016 Rank | Company Name, City, Province | Total Design Revenue', and the row reads '12 | 12 | Shanghai Municipal Engineering Design Institute (Group) Co. Ltd., Shanghai | $367.13'. The page's introduction gives the basis as 'revenue for design services performed in $ millions' and attaches no fiscal year to any row, so the undated figure is right and the writer was right not to take 2017 or 2016 off the table's title. CORRECTED: 'Engineering design firm' to 'Chinese design firm'. 'Engineering' was being read off the company's own name, which is the restatement fault; what the page itself supplies is the classification 'Chinese design firm' (the list's title and scope) and the city column. Still not written: owner, parent group, state ownership, founding year, staff count, country count, any listing. I re-ran the writer's route report and it holds — a fresh search returned Devex, DevelopmentAid, structurae, a market-data aggregator (moomoo) and a conference sponsor page, all barred, and no reachable company site or filing. Kept rather than blanked because the sector, the city and the revenue are all on the page; it remains the thinnest of the four and rests on one trade-press row.

codesc.name: Athi Water Works Development Agency
codesc.desc: Kenyan state water agency, one of the water works development agencies established by the Cabinet Secretary for Water and Sanitation under section 65(1) of the Water Act by Legal Notice 28 of 2019, with Nairobi, Kiambu and Murang'a counties as its area. Its own account of its mandate is the development, maintenance and management of national public water works, and operating them as a water service provider until the assets are handed over to a county provider.

sources.title: The Establishment of Water Works Development Agencies (Legal Notice 28 of 2019)
sources.publisher: Kenya Law (national gazette text, Government of Kenya)

sources.title: About AWWDA
sources.publisher: Athi Water Works Development Agency (Government of Kenya)

codesc.note: Checked, and rewritten onto the instrument rather than the website. The gazette notice itself was opened on Kenya Law: 'The Establishment of Water Works Development Agencies', Legal Notice 28 of 2019, made under section 65(1) of the Water Act (Cap. 372) by the Cabinet Secretary for Water and Sanitation, commenced 3 May 2019, with the entry for Athi Water Works Development Agency giving its jurisdiction as Nairobi, Kiambu and Murang'a Counties. The agency's own About page was also re-opened and the writer's quotations from it are accurate. CORRECTED, three claims that the notice does not carry and that the website carries in a form the notice contradicts: (a) 'one of nine water works development agencies' — the notice establishes EIGHT; the count is dropped rather than reconciled, and both figures are recorded here. (b) 'under the Ministry of Water, Sanitation and Irrigation' — the notice names no parent ministry, only the Cabinet Secretary for Water and Sanitation. 'X sits under Y' needed a document that says it and the gazette does not, so the ministry is out and the Cabinet Secretary who made the notice is in, which is what is documented. (c) the day '26 April 2019' — the website's date; Kenya Law gives publication and commencement on 3 May 2019. The day is dropped, the year kept. Also dropped: 'develops and runs national public water works in Nairobi, Kiambu and Murang'a counties' as a single assertion, which welded the website's function list onto the area — the functions are now given as the agency's own account and the area as the notice's. Not written, as the writer also declined: the page's 5,800.4 km2 and 9,320,287 population, which describe the territory and not the agency; and anything about the predecessor Athi Water Services Board — neither the notice nor the About page mentions it, so the succession is still unsourced. REJECTED CORRECTION, and it runs the other way from the writer's report: the writer flagged the card's role text ('under the Ministry of Water and Sanitation') as conflicting with the agency's page ('Water, Sanitation and Irrigation'). The gazette's own wording is 'Cabinet Secretary for Water and Sanitation', which is the card's form, so the card should not be changed on that point. The agency's page is the later ministry name. Route not landed: the Auditor-General's report on the agency, catalogued at the Kenyan parliament library, was not read, and it is the route to a staff, budget or revenue figure and to the succession from the Services Board.

codesc.name: China Gezhouba Group Corporation (CGGC)
codesc.desc: Chinese water-conservancy, hydropower and large-infrastructure builder, grown out of the bureau that built the Gezhouba dam on the Yangtze from December 1970. China's Belt and Road Portal says it was listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 1997 and became an unlisted joint-stock company in 2021 after China Energy Engineering Corporation Limited (Energy China) acquired and merged it by share swap, and gives its revenue for 2020 as RMB 115 billion.

sources.title: CGGC of Energy China
sources.publisher: Belt and Road Portal, Government of China (eng.yidaiyilu.gov.cn)

codesc.note: Checked. The page was re-opened and it does name the company exactly as the key does, 'China Gezhouba Group Corporation (CGGC)', calls it 'a joint-stock limited company', dates the start of Gezhouba dam construction to 1970.12.30, the renaming to 330 Engineering Bureau to 1974, attaches 'Listed on the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 1997' to CGGC in its opening paragraph, and says 'CGGC became an unlisted joint-stock company after it was acquired and merged by China Energy Engineering Corporation Limited (Energy China) via stock swap' in 2021. The 2020 figures are attached to 2020 in one sentence: contract amount RMB 300 billion, revenue RMB 115 billion, total profits RMB 8.6 billion. So every fact was on the page. CORRECTED: the writer's desc asserted the 1997 listing, the 2021 delisting and the revenue in the map's own voice while the writer's own note said they were attributed to the page. This is where fault 3 lands — the entity listed in Shanghai and absorbed by Energy China in 2021 was the separately incorporated China Gezhouba Group Co., Ltd., and this government page runs the parent and that listed arm together as one story, which the writer saw and recorded. The attribution has been moved into the desc itself, so a reader is told whose statement the listing chain is. Also corrected: 'from 1970' to 'from December 1970', which is the date the page gives. Not written, as the writer also declined: the page's 'national team' and 'global business card' phrasing, 'over 5,000 projects', '100 world records', and the 2016 'exceeded and maintained at more than RMB one hundred billion' line, which attaches to no single year. The 1994 group named on the page (China Gezhouba Water Conservancy and Hydropower Engineering Group Corporation) is presented there as the sponsoring group rather than as this company, so it is not written either.

complaints.al: Police opened fire on villagers protesting at Gondamara on 4 April 2016, killing four and wounding 30; a February 2017 clash between pro- and anti-plant factions killed one man and injured 16. Police killed five workers protesting unpaid wages on 17 April 2021 and two more died of their injuries, a toll of seven; an engineer was arrested on 28 May 2021 under the Digital Security Act over a Facebook post. Bank of China, China Development Bank, China Construction Bank, Agricultural Bank of China, China Minsheng Bank and Rupali Bank signed a US$1.782 billion buyer's credit on 28 December 2018, insured by Sinosure.
complaints.fi: AidData records the Chinese financing and summarizes press and NGO reports of harm; it makes no finding of its own.

complaints.t: Java 9 and 10 loan, pollution and protests
complaints.pt: Suralaya Power Station complex, the card's coordinate (Wikipedia)
complaints.al: As construction began on units 9 and 10, residents complained of already high air pollution from the plant and damage to the sea and the local fishing industry; demonstrations followed in January and April 2021. A Greenpeace model from November 2019 projected 4,700 premature deaths over the plant's life, and WALHI sued over the environmental permit in November 2020. Eleven banks including Bank of China signed a US$2.6 billion loan on 17 July 2020, secured by a pledge of shares in PT Barito Wahana Tenaga.
complaints.fi: AidData records the Chinese financing and summarizes press and NGO reports of harm; it makes no finding of its own.

complaints.t: Thar Block II mine syndicated loan
complaints.place: Thar Block II, near Islamkot, Tharparkar, Sindh, Pakistan
complaints.pt: Approximate: Thar Block II mine-mouth power station, the card's coordinate (Global Energy Monitor)
complaints.al: ICBC, China Construction Bank and China Development Bank signed a US$200 million syndicated loan to Sindh Engro Coal Mining Company on 21 December 2015, over 14 years at six-month LIBOR plus a 3.3% margin, with a 6.616% Sinosure premium, a Pakistani sovereign guarantee and a pledge of the company's shares. It funded a coal mine of 3.8 million tonnes a year in Thar Block II, 25 km from Islamkot near the village of Singharo-Bitra, supplying a 2 x 330 MW mine-mouth power plant; the project cost US$911 million, work began on 13 April 2016 and commercial operation on 10 July 2019.
complaints.fi: AidData records the Chinese financing and the project timeline only; it describes no harm and makes no finding of its own.
